description: We’re Tec it Easy, a team of students from Tecnológico de Monterrey who enjoy learning, sharing ideas, and solving problems together. Our interests include AI, data science, programming, and design. We bring curiosity, creativity, and a collaborative mindset, and we’re excited to explore space science while building something meaningful.
summary:
What should we plant next? I built Heirloom with my grandfather, a farmer in Veracruz, Mexico, in mind. I wanted to see how a view of Earth from space could inform a decision he makes on the ground: what to plant next and what that choice could mean for the seasons that follow.

Heirloom is a tool for exploring crop rotations. Farmers start with a location and describe what they already grow, when they can plant, and which crops are practical for them. That local knowledge helps shape the alternatives they can compare with their current practice.

For the demo in Jesús Carranza, Veracruz, I used 20 years of NASA POWER weather data (2005–2024) to evaluate crop sequences across 18 overlapping three-year periods. A daily water balance based on FAO-56 estimates when crops could face water shortages and how those shortages might affect potential yields. Running the same sequences through different historical periods lets farmers see how the comparison changes with the weather.

The goal is to help farmers decide which options are worth exploring before committing a season to them. The next step is to compare the model’s estimates with field measurements and farmers’ observations.
details:
Heirloom helps farmers explore what to plant over several seasons. The guided workflow starts with a location and asks about the farmer’s current crops, planting calendar, and which alternatives are feasible. The farmer’s current practice can serve as a baseline for comparing other crop sequences over the same period.

In the Jesús Carranza pilot, I used daily NASA POWER weather records from 2005 to 2024. I organized them into 18 overlapping three-year windows, from 2005–2007 through 2022–2024. The prototype applies a daily water balance based on FAO-56 to estimate water stress and its potential effect on relative yield. Evaluating the same sequences across those windows shows how sensitive the comparison is to the weather each sequence encounters.

What makes Heirloom different is the combination of historical weather and the farmer’s own knowledge of what can actually be planted. A grower can use the comparison to identify which rotations are worth discussing or testing locally. I built the web interface with Next.js and used a separate Python engine for the calculations.

The historical pilot produced preliminary estimates for water stress. The next step is to check those estimates against field observations and measurements, then extend the comparison to cover heat stress, soil health, and farm economics.
